messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tane, a 63‑year‑old pilot of New Zealand descent, recounts the night he first felt the sky itself betray him. During a night raid on a hostile outpost, his helicopter was suddenly struck by a missile that splashed burning fuel across the cockpit. The impact shattered his world in seconds: a searing heat, a jagged scrape of metal against his hands, the unmistakable hiss of the helicopter’s rotors, and a sudden, inexplicable texture of cold, rough metal that left his fingers numb. He woke hours later, the smell of ozone clinging to his skin, and the image of that texture replaying in his mind as if it were someone else’s nightmare. The tactile texture that pressed against his skin, the exact hour of the attack—2 a.m.—and the relentless roar of aircraft engines in the distance have become more than memories; they are triggers that plunge Tane into a state of heightened threat. When he feels the roughness of a rough‑textured seat on the airplane, or hears the distant hum of a jet’s engine at 2 p.m., he instantly scans the cockpit for exits, feels his pulse race, and believes the world is about to strike again. The same sensations also fuel his belief that something is fundamentally wrong with him; he is convinced his own mind has betrayed him, that he has lost the happiness he once knew, and that the world is a dangerous place that will inevitably crush him again. These negative appraisals of self, happiness, and safety do more than shape his perception; they amplify the sense of threat and reinforce the triggers. When Tane thinks he is defective, the texture of a rough seat becomes more ominous, and the sound of aircraft engines becomes a louder, more menacing call. The belief that the world is unsafe makes the mere sight of a helicopter alarmingly familiar, tightening his vigilance and pushing him further into fear. The memory of that night is alien, as if it were another person’s story, yet it erupts with the same terror he felt on the ground. The vivid recall of the explosion and the texture of hot metal on his fingers triggers a rush of panic that feels instantaneous and unavoidable. In the quiet moments between flights, the memory surfaces without warning, its terror spilling over into his thoughts and making him feel as though the past is happening again. The memory also reinforces his negative self‑views, reinforcing the sense that he is defective and that he can never feel safe. Night vigilance—a core component of his threat appraisal—spills back into the memory and the triggers, creating a vicious cycle. When he is awake at night, he cannot find a place to rest; his mind is perpetually scanning, and the sight of a distant aircraft or the rough texture of a new flight seat snaps him back to the memory of the missile strike. That memory, in turn, sharpens his sense of danger, making the next trigger even more frightening. Because of this relentless loop, Tane has begun to avoid flying at night, preferring daylight hours even when the schedule demands otherwise. He has declined several flight assignments, missing out on promotions, and his wife has begun to worry that he will never again feel the freedom he once enjoyed at 30,000 feet. The constant self‑doubt has eroded the joy he once found in soaring, and he now feels an ever‑growing sense that his career and his happiness are both fragile and doomed. It is this compounding sense of loss and dread that has finally pushed Tane to seek help. He fears that if he does not find a way to break this cycle, he will never again taste the thrill of a clear night sky, and he longs to reclaim the sense of safety that once allowed him to trust his own judgment. He hopes that, with the right support, he can untangle the painful links that bind his triggers, threat, memory, and negative beliefs, and learn to fly once more without the shadow of that night hanging over him.
